extracted.intended_audience: biologists, geneticists, and statisticians studying quantitative heredity / students of evolutionary biology
extracted.subtask_description: Methods and measurable criteria for quantifying heredity (direct and cross), predicting offspring traits from parental data, and testing phenomena such as prepotency, telegony, and inheritance of fertility using correlation and regression techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct vs cross heredity (definition and measurement)
rubrics_metrics.description: If x and y be the same organ, we are said to investigate the direct heredity between A and B; if x and y be different organs we deal with the cross heredity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the chosen organ(s) in many pairs of relatives and form a correlation table exactly as for other traits (example: stature father→son). Ensure you measure the same organ for direct heredity comparisons; use large samples (e.g. ~1000 pairs) for stable estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coefficient of heredity (correlation r)
rubrics_metrics.description: The coefficient of correlation r, as determined from a correlation table for organs of A and B, is the coefficient of heredity — the quantitative measure of heredity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute r from the correlation table (see p.397 referenced). Example given: r = .396 for father→son stature. Use r to predict average resemblance between relatives, and to compute related quantities (regression, offspring variability). Beware assortative mating which may inflate r.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regression equation for predicting offspring (regression line)
rubrics_metrics.description: The regression equation gives the probable stature (or trait) of the offspring from a parent of given stature: e.g. 'stature of son — 69.25 = .446 × (stature of father — 69.11)', so stature of son = 38.45 + .446 × stature of father.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat regression predictions as probabilistic group statements — 'do not expect... that this result will apply to every individual case.' Apply to large samples (e.g., fifty fathers of same height) to compare averages. Use the regression coefficient derived from the correlation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regression toward the mean (interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fathers of extreme stature produce sons nearer the population mean: exceptional parents are rare while mediocre parents are common, so an exceptional individual is more likely to arise from mediocre parents than from exceptional parents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use population ancestry size reasoning (e.g., many ancestors dilute extremes) to interpret regression; selection removing mediocre ancestry (as breeders do) can reduce regression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offspring variability given parental selection (sd scaling)
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard-deviation of an array of offspring corresponding to a parent of given value is the population standard-deviation multiplied by sqrt(1 − r^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: with r = .396, multiply population sd by 0.9183 — selection of fathers reduces sons' variability by ~8%. Use this to quantify how parental selection changes offspring variability; biologists should treat selection effects as definite, calculable amounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing and using empirical correlation tables (sample size & comparability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form correlation tables for measured organs of pairs of relatives (example: 1000 such pairs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use large, comparable samples and consistent measurement procedures. Control or account for environmental differences (e.g., periodic selection acting on sons before they become fathers). Where environmental control is impossible, interpret coefficients cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected intensity ranges by relationship (benchmarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Average intensities: parental (about .3 to .5), grandparental (about .15 to .3), fraternal (about .4 to .6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these ranges as theoretical/empirical benchmarks for blended inheritance; note fraternal correlations are somewhat reduced for opposite-sex pairs. Compare observed coefficients with these ranges to assess consistency with theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assortative mating (measurement and effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: The correlation between father's and mother's organs measures the intensity of assortative mating (homogamy), which strongly influences observed heredity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In datasets where spouse correlation is high, expect increased parent–offspring correlation. Account for assortative mating when interpreting coefficients of heredity; Pearson attributes high father–son r in one series to assortative mating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepotency (test via comparative coefficients)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepotency can be settled by investigating whether there is a sensible difference between the coefficients of heredity determined in the usual manner for given organs and pairs of relatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare paternal vs maternal coefficients (e.g., father vs mother contribution to offspring). Examples: father prepotent for stature; male often transmits more than female for several traits. But exercise caution: differences may arise from non-biological causes (e.g., non-paternity) or living/handling conditions of pedigree animals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex-specific inheritance rules (empirical patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical rules: (b) intensity of heredity often stronger in son than daughter; (c) same-sex relatives resemble each other more than opposite-sex pairs; (d) inheritance down a single-sex line shows prepotency over cross-sex line (e.g., man resembles paternal grandfather more than maternal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check multiple characters (stature, head-index, eye-colour, coat-colour). Don't infer causal mechanisms hastily; account for possible sampling or sociocultural confounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing for telegony (operational criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: To detect telegony (influence of prior male on later ova), measure the intensity of heredity between both parents and elder vs younger children and look for a steady increase in paternal influence or decrease in maternal influence over successive offspring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: stature data for elder vs younger sons/daughters show no increase in paternal influence — no evidence for steady telegenic effect. Isolated zebra/horse anecdotes insufficient; look for consistent trends across many families. Beware rare abnormal preservation of earlier gametes which could mimic telegony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inheritance of fertility/fecundity (treat fertility as a measurable character)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat annual fertility or fecundity analogously to other characters: form correlation tables for pairs of relatives living under similar environments to estimate heritability coefficients (e.g., mother–daughter, paternal grandmother–granddaughter, father–son).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control for social/customary factors (age at marriage, duration of marriage, marital restraint) which mask constitutional fertility. Use only marriages lasting sufficient years (text uses ≥15 years as a baseline) to get minimum heritability; reported coefficients: mother–daughter = .213 ± .020, paternal grandmother–granddaughter = .112 ± .021, father–son = .116 ± .021. Interpret these as minimum estimates due to measurement limits and monogamy confounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing fecundity vs fertility and measurement limits in stud records
rubrics_metrics.description: Fecundity (e.g., ratio of surviving foals to possible foals) may be the measurable quantity in studbooks rather than total fertility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When total fertility cannot be ascertained, use fecundity measures with caution; expect additional complications due to breeding practices. Example: thoroughbred horses show fecundity inherited dam→daughter and via sire to daughters (latent male fecundity measurable through daughter outcomes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genetic selection (conceptual criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: If fertility/fecundity are inheritable, differential fertility is the basis of genetic selection; if the most fertile are not the most fit for the environment, genetic selection can change population composition rapidly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use demographic and heritability data (class fertility rates, marriage rates, selective death-rates) to assess potential for genetic selection. The author cites Danish data showing working classes have higher absolute fertility; consider societal implications and policy consequences (e.g., restraint of fertility affecting fitter classes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for non-genetic confounds (non-paternity, social customs, selection before measurement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed reductions/changes in heredity intensity may reflect non-genetic factors: e.g., low father–child correlation could indicate non-paternity; reductions in expected coefficients may reflect social screening or periodic selection acting on sons before fatherhood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly check and, where possible, quantify non-genetic sources (conjugal fidelity, marital duration, selective mortality). The text gives Boas' caution about looseness of family relations as an interpretation of low coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bi-parental inheritance modelling (partial regression coefficients)
rubrics_metrics.description: When both parents are considered, the mean type of the offspring array consists of two terms proportional to parental deviations: μ3 = c1 × h1 + c2 × h2 where c1 and c2 are partial regression coefficients determined from parental and offspring correlations and variabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute c1 and c2 algebraically from correlations r (paternal), r' (maternal), and r_parent_parent (assortative mating), and compute offspring variability 2 using the given formulae. Special case: equipotent parents (r1 = r2) gives symmetric partial regressions and specific expressions for S^2. Use full algebraic derivations (text gives formulae) rather than ad hoc weighting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical epistemology (group vs individual predictions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The statistician dealing with heredity can say little or nothing of the individual; his knowledge is of the group containing great numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not over-interpret regression/prediction results at the individual level. Use statistical statements as statements about average probable resemblance across groups; ensure large N for inference.
